```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(metacheck)
psychsci <- papers_load("psychsci", cache = TRUE)
```

The first step to using Metacheck is to read in a manuscript. Metacheck converts PDF files with bibr or GROBID. If you have a manuscript in a different format, save a copy as a PDF (bibr can also convert DOC and DOCX files, but only on the Scienceverse platform or your own bibr server). You have two options to convert a PDF. First, you can use a local version of GROBID. We will explain this below, but it requires more technical knowledge, and sufficient space on your harddrive. Alternatively, you can use an online server. This is much simpler, and it is the approach we use by default in this manual. Nevertheless, you might prefer not to send your manuscript to an external server, or you might not be allowed to. We have developed Metacheck to always work locally, without an internet connection, to also make it available in these more restrictive situations.

The function `convert()` can read PDF files and save them in [JSON format](https://www.scienceverse.org/schema/paper.json). This requires an internet connection and takes a few seconds per paper. The conversion process needs to be done only once and the converted file can be saved for later use. If you don't supply an `api_url`, `api_key` or `backend`, Metacheck sends the PDF to its own server on SURF Research Cloud in the Netherlands, which converts it with bibr when bibr is available and otherwise with GROBID on the same server, needs no API key, deletes the uploaded PDF once it is converted, and deletes the result an hour later. That server converts whole PDFs without figures, of at most 50 MB. If it cannot be reached, Metacheck uses a local GROBID server, then a local bibr server, and then the first available server in a [list of active servers](https://www.scienceverse.org/metacheck/convert.json). You can set another address for the SURF server with the `SURF_API_URL` environment variable.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pdf_file <- demofile("pdf")
json_file <- convert(file_path = pdf_file,
                     save_path = "converted")
```

You can also supplement the reference list with information retrieved from CrossRef. This can increase the accuracy of the information in the reference list. Retrieving this information also requires an internet connection, and can take some time. Add it after you have read the paper in (see below) with the `add_bib_match()` function: `paper <- add_bib_match(paper)`. The argument `crossref_lookup = TRUE` of `convert()` does the same, but only when the PDF is converted with GROBID (`method = "grobid"`) or when you convert a GROBID XML file; with the default SURF server it has no effect.

```{r, include = FALSE}
# doesn't require a call to the grobid server
json_file <- demofile("json")
```

## Local conversion through GROBID in Docker

You can set up your own local GROBID server following instructions from <https://grobid.readthedocs.io/>. The easiest way is to use Docker. The following code installs GROBID 0.9.1 (the official image, without deep-learning models; it needs about 4 GB of memory) if you run it in your system terminal.

``` bash
docker run --rm --init --ulimit core=0 -p 8070:8070 grobid/grobid:0.9.1-crf
```

Set `method = "grobid"` and the `api_url` to the local path <http://localhost:8070> (as illustrated below) to convert with the local GROBID server. Metacheck only picks a local GROBID server by itself when the SURF server cannot be reached, so name it whenever the manuscript must stay on your computer.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
json_file <- convert(file_path = pdf_file,
                     save_path = "converted",
                     method = "grobid",
                     api_url = "http://localhost:8070")
```

If you run your own bibr server instead, name it in the same way: `convert(pdf_file, method = "bibr", api_url = "http://localhost:8000")`. `convert_bibr()`, the function `convert()` calls for bibr, also reads the address from the `BIBR_API_URL` environment variable, but `convert()` itself only skips the SURF server when `api_url`, `api_key` or `backend` is given. A bibr server that requires a token, as `bibr serve` does in production mode, gets it from `api_key` or the `BIBR_API_KEY` environment variable.

## Load from JSON or XML

The function `read()` reads in papers created by `convert()`. It accepts both the **bibr JSON** files and the **GROBID XML** (TEI) files that conversion produces, so you can use whichever you have.

```{r}
# read a converted JSON file
paper <- read(json_file)
```

```{r}
# read a GROBID XML file directly
paper_xml <- read(demofile("xml"))
```

## Batch Processing

The functions `convert()` and `read()` also work on a folder of files, or a vector of paths, returning a list of JSON file paths or paper objects, respectively. Batch processing is especially useful for scientists who want to be able to examine a large number of manuscripts. For example, a metascientist might be interesting in examining the uptake of open science practices over time, and run Metacheck across all articles published in a scientific journal. As part of Metacheck, we have created a paper repository of more than 15.000 open access articles that you can read in through the function `papers_load()`. See [Using the Paper Database Corpora](papers-databases.qmd) for how to load the available corpora.

When a folder contains both a `.json` and a `.xml` file for the same paper, `read()` uses the JSON and skips the duplicate XML. Papers in a list that share a `paper_id` are renamed `"<paper_id>~2"`, `"<paper_id>~3"`, and so on, with a warning, when the list is made (`paperlist()`) or used (`module_run()`, `report()`), because results are joined by `paper_id` and papers with the same id would be mixed up. `read()` refuses a JSON file that is not bibr output (for example one without a `paper_id`), skipping it with a warning.

## The paper object

`read()` returns a **paper object**: a structured representation of the manuscript, stored as a list of tables. Everything Metacheck does — searching text, running modules, checking references — operates on this object, so it is worth understanding what is inside it and how to get at each piece.

A paper object has the class `scivrs_paper`, and you access its parts with the `$` operator. Here are all the components:

```{r}
class(paper)
names(paper)
```

The components are summarised below; the rest of this section shows each one. Most are data frames, so you can work with them using base R or the tidyverse.

| Component | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `paper_id` | A single string identifying the paper |
| `info` | One row of paper-level metadata (title, DOI, type, ...) |
| `author` | One row per author |
| `text` | One row per sentence |
| `section` | One row per heading/section |
| `url` | Links found in the text |
| `bib` | The reference list |
| `xref` | Cross-references linking sentences to bib entries, tables, and figures |
| `figure` | Figures |
| `table` | Tables |
| `eq` | Extracted statistics and equations |
| `bib_match` | Reference metadata matched from CrossRef and other services |

**paper_id**

A single string identifying the paper (the user-supplied id, the DOI, or the filename):

```{r}
paper$paper_id
```

**info**

A one-row data frame of paper-level metadata. Use `t()` to read it as a column:

```{r}
t(paper$info) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = "value")
```

Pull out a single field directly:

```{r}
paper$info$title
paper$info$doi
```

**author**

One row per author, in paper order:

```{r}
paper$author[, c("given", "family", "affiliation", "corresponding")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**text**

One row per sentence (excluding the title, headings, and references). This is the table that `text_search()` searches.

```{r}
nrow(paper$text)
head(paper$text[, c("text", "section_id", "paragraph_id")]) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**section**

One row per heading. `section_type` is Metacheck's best guess at the kind of section, which modules use to focus on (say) only the results:

```{r}
paper$section[, c("section_id", "header", "section_type")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**url**

Every external link found in the text, with the sentence (`text_id`) it appeared in:

```{r}
paper$url |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**bib**

The reference list, parsed into columns:

```{r}
paper$bib[, c("bib_id", "authors", "year", "title")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**xref**

Cross-references that link a sentence (`text_id`) to an item it cites — a bib entry, table, or figure (`xref_type`):

```{r}
paper$xref |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**figure and table**

Figures and tables each get a row, linked to the `section` table by `section_id`:

```{r}
paper$figure[, c("figure_id", "section_id", "page_number")] |>
  knitr::kable()
paper$table[, c("table_id", "section_id", "page_number")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**eq**

Statistics and equations extracted from the text, broken into a left-hand side, degrees of freedom, comparator, and right-hand side. Many statistics modules read from this table rather than re-scanning the text:

```{r}
head(paper$eq) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**bib_match**

When you run `add_bib_match()`, or convert with GROBID and `crossref_lookup = TRUE` (or run a reference module), Metacheck matches each reference against services like CrossRef and stores the retrieved metadata here, keyed by `bib_id`:

```{r}
paper$bib_match[, c("bib_id", "service", "doi", "title")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Working with a list of papers

A *paperlist* is simply a list of paper objects — for example the `psychsci` corpus (250 open-access *Psychological Science* articles, loaded with `papers_load("psychsci", cache = TRUE)` — see [Using the Paper Database Corpora](papers-databases.qmd)). To pull the same component from every paper into one combined table, use `paper_table()`:

```{r}
paper_table(psychsci[1:5], "info", c("title", "doi")) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Most functions and every module accept either a single paper or a paperlist, so the same code scales from one paper to a whole corpus. See [Using the Paper Database Corpora](papers-databases.qmd) for the available corpora.
